pages.title: WELCOME TO GREEK ROOTS
content: English keeps its serious words in Greek:
the sciences, medicine, the theatre, the
church, and a surprising number of the
plain ones. School, idea, music and panic
are Greek. So are television and dinosaur.
Most of them are built from parts. Learn
a part once and every word that carries it
opens: tele- is far, so telephone, telescope
and television are far-voice, far-sight and
far-seeing before you look them up.
This pack teaches the parts, root by root,
and the famous words that carry them. You
need no Greek. You need to notice.

pages.title: HOW A CARD WORKS
content: The front shows a word. Press a key and the
card opens in stages: a sentence that uses
it, its DEFINITION, a second example built
on a cousin word, and, on 8, the notes.
The notes are the point of this pack. They
show the parts and what each part means:
tele- (far) + PHONE (φωνή, voice)
The Greek word sits beside its part in the
original letters. You do not read Greek;
you learn to recognise it.
Rate the card 0 to 5 when it is open. The
boss fight asks the definition and offers
eight words; the notes' synonyms and
antonyms are the clues you take with you.
THE FIRST TWENTY are the famous ones:
television, telescope, dinosaur, helicopter,
hippopotamus, democracy, philosophy. Each
comes apart in the hand, and each carries
one line of its story.
THEN the words English took from Greek
whole, and after them the machinery: tele-
and auto-, bio- and graph, micro- and
-scope, cluster by cluster.
Every cluster opens with a short lesson
naming its parts. The last cluster of the
pack is the exam: twenty monsters that fall
apart the moment you see the parts.
THE NEXT 20 CARDS: the famous twenty.
These twenty came into English whole.
Nothing was joined to anything: English
took the Greek noun and kept it, and the
sense moved on over the centuries.
school     σχολή    leisure
idea       ἰδέα     form
panic      πανικόν  of Pan
chaos      χάος     a yawning gap
Schole was the free time a citizen gave
to discussion, then the discussion, then
the building. Chaos was the empty gap
before the world, not disorder.
THE NEXT 20 CARDS: Greek taken whole.
TELE (τῆλε) means far. AUTO (αὐτός) means
self. Both bolt onto almost any stem,
Greek or not.
telepathy   far + feeling
teleport    far + carry
autopilot   self + steersman
automaton   self + willing
Half of them are hybrids: teleport and
automobile take Latin second halves,
telecast an Old Norse one. The prefix
does not mind what it is joined to.
THE NEXT 16 CARDS: tele- and auto-.
CYCL (κύκλος) is a circle or a wheel.
DYNAM (δύναμις) is power.
cycle        a round, a circle
cyclone      a coiling wind
dynamic      power + relating to
dynamite     power + substance
Cyclops is round-eye, cycl plus ops.
Dynasty is the odd one out: power held
inside one family, nothing mechanical.
Half the wheels are hybrids. Unicycle,
motorcycle and recycle all take Latin
first halves.
THE NEXT 12 CARDS: cycl and dynam.
GRAPH (γράφειν) is to write or draw. BIO
(βίος) is life. Greek will fuse two roots
with nothing in between.
telegraph    far + writing
phonograph   sound + writing
biology      life + study
biography    life + writing
The instruments follow the rule: a
polygraph writes many signals at once, a
seismograph writes the shaking.
Biopsy is not bio plus a psy. It is bio
plus opsis, sight: a look at the living.
THE NEXT 14 CARDS: bio and graph.
MICRO (μικρός) is small. The ending
-SCOPE (σκόπιον) is an instrument for
looking, from skopein, to watch.
microbe      small + life
microscope   small + viewer
periscope    around + viewer
stethoscope  chest + viewer
A microwave is not a small oven; the
wave is short. Horoscope keeps the old
sense, an observer of the hour.
THE NEXT 11 CARDS: micro- and -scope.
PHOTO (φῶς, phos) is light. GEO (γῆ) is
earth. Both stand in front and name what
the second part works on.
photon       light + particle
photocopy    light + copy
geology      earth + study
geometry     earth + measuring
Photo on its own is a clipped
photograph, light-writing.
Geometry began as surveying, the
measuring of fields. Photogenic once
meant produced by light, not pretty.
THE NEXT 12 CARDS: photo- and geo-.
The Greek numbers count what a word is
made of: MONO (μόνος) one, DI (δίς) two,
TRI (τρεῖς) three, TETRA (τέτταρες) four.
monologue    one + speech
dilemma      two + premises
tripod       three + feet
tetralogy    four + works
The two in diploma is not a pair but a
fold: a diploma was a paper folded
double, and diplomacy is named after
those same folded papers.
Latin counts as well. Unicycle is Latin
one on a Greek wheel.
THE NEXT 19 CARDS: mono- to tetra-.
PENTA five, HEXA six, HEPTA seven, OCTA
eight, DECA ten: πέντε, ἕξ, ἑπτά, ὀκτώ,
δέκα. Then -GON (γωνία) is an angle and
athlon is a contest.
pentagon     five + angles
heptathlon   seven + contests
octahedron   eight + faces
decade       ten + a group
HEMI (ἡμι-) is half and POLY (πολύς) is
many: a hemisphere is half a ball, a
polygon has as many angles as it likes.
Hexadecimal is a mongrel, Greek six on
Latin ten, for base sixteen.
THE NEXT 15 CARDS: five to ten.
MEGA (μέγας) is great and MACRO (μακρός)
is large. The metric prefixes KILO
(χίλιοι) thousand and HECTO (ἑκατόν)
hundred are Greek numbers put to work in
the measuring system.
megaphone     great + voice
megalomania   greatness + madness
kilometre     thousand + measure
macrocosm     large + world
In science mega- is exactly a million
and kilo- exactly a thousand; in speech
mega just means big. Micro- is the
opposite of macro-, not of mega-.
THE NEXT 18 CARDS: mega-, kilo-, macro-.
PHONE (φωνή) is sound or voice. METER
(μέτρον) is a measure. Both come last,
and the first part says which sound, or
what is being measured.
symphony     together + sound
cacophony    bad + sound
diameter     across + measure
perimeter    around + measure
A xylophone sounds wood, a barometer
measures weight, an odometer measures
the road.
Saxophone and speedometer are built the
same way on words that are not Greek.
THE NEXT 17 CARDS: -phone and -meter.
LOGOS (λόγος) is word, reason, account;
as an ending, -OLOGY is the study of a
thing. MANIA (μανία) is madness.
psychology    mind + study
theology      god + study
kleptomania   stealing + madness
pyromania     fire + madness
The first part is usually Greek too:
anthropo- human, chrono- time, zoo-
animal. Sociology is the hybrid, Latin
socius on a Greek ending.
Mania alone is a fit of frenzy; -mania
on the end of a word is a compulsion.
THE NEXT 17 CARDS: -ology and -mania.
ANTI (ἀντί) is against, HYPER (ὑπέρ) is
over or beyond, PSEUDO (ψεῦδος) false.
antibiotic   against + life
antagonist   against + contender
hyperbole    beyond + a throwing
pseudonym    false + name
All three will attach to anything
English has: antifreeze, antivirus,
hyperlink, pseudoscience.
Hyper- is above normal and hypo- is
below it: hypertension is high blood
pressure, hypotension is low.
THE NEXT 20 CARDS: against, over, false.
